The Markov property

The bandits of Lessons 5 to 14 had no situation that carried over from one step to the next. Full RL does, and it rests on one assumption about it: the present state holds everything about the past that matters for the future. That is the Markov property. Whether it holds depends on what you choose to call the state.

40,000 days of weather from one of two towns. Click the days to set a history. The green box is the state. Compare the forecast from the whole history with the forecast from the state alone. Start with two rainy days in Town A, then switch to Town B.

The maths

Let $S_t$ be the state on day $t$. The state has the Markov property if

$$P(S_{t+1} \mid S_t) = P(S_{t+1} \mid S_1, S_2, \dots, S_t)$$

Once you know today, knowing every earlier day changes nothing about tomorrow. The present screens off the past.

In Town A the weather follows this rule, with $S_t$ = today's weather. Any extra days you add to the history leave the forecast where it was, up to sampling noise.

In Town B, rain rarely lasts more than two days: after two wet days the clouds usually clear. Today's weather alone is then not Markov, because yesterday changes the forecast. The fix is to put the missing information into the state:

$$S'_t = (\text{yesterday}, \text{today}) = (W_{t-1}, W_t)$$

$W_t$ is the weather on day $t$. With $S'_t$ as the state, Town B is Markov again. The price is more states: $3^2 = 9$ instead of 3, and $3^k$ if the town remembered $k$ days.

In RL the property is stated for the environment's response to an action (S&B §3.1). The next state and reward depend only on the current state and action:

$$\begin{aligned} &P(S_{t+1}, R_{t+1} \mid S_t, A_t) \\ &\quad = P(S_{t+1}, R_{t+1} \mid S_0, A_0, R_1, \dots, S_t, A_t) \end{aligned}$$

A chess position is Markov: how the pieces got there does not matter. A single frame of a video game usually is not, because it shows where the ball is but not where it is going. DQN (Lesson 66) fixes this the Town B way, stacking the last 4 frames into one state.
